title: The Blue Wave Lifted Democrats. But Not All Progressives Rose as High.
summary: The performance gap with moderates narrowed, but progressive candidates underperformed by enough to keep the “electability” debate alive.

Democrats have been debating whether the party should move to the left or the center for nearly a decade. This month’s midterm results were almost perfectly calibrated to make sure the debate rages into the next presidential primary.


On the one hand, Democrats[won in a tsunami](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/upshot/democrats-midterm-elections-trump-tsunami.html) . They often did so with a populist pitch, and despite the calls for the party to move to the center. The new progressive activist left won more races than ever before, including its first big victory in a battleground state: Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed won a divisive race for Senate. Incredibly, in May, he even[predicted](https://x.com/AbdulElSayed/status/2051104145474466216)[his exact margin](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-michigan-us-senate.html) of victory: seven percentage points.


On the other hand, progressive candidates underperformed by enough and in enough races to keep the old “electability” debate alive and well. Many of the weakest Democratic results — those where the party fared relatively poorly given the national environment and the characteristics of the state or district — came in races where Democrats picked progressive candidates in contested nominating fights this summer.


Mr. El-Sayed’s victory is an example of this kind of underperformance. While he won and won comfortably, his victory was underwhelming if judged against how Democrats did elsewhere in the country. After all, Michigan usually votes about the same as the country; this year, Democrats are on track to win by 13 or 14 points nationwide. Mr. El-Sayed’s seven-point victory counts as a significant underperformance against that backdrop.


It’s important to note that many progressives fared well, even though many of the party’s weakest showings featured progressive nominees. In congressional races in Montana, Ohio and Pennsylvania, populists with a blue-collar background — like firefighters and union leaders — won in districts that voted for President Trump in the last election. Progressives also fared extraordinarily well, like Democrats of all political stripes, in districts with large Hispanic populations, including in key battlegrounds in California and Colorado.


And if one accepts a broad definition of progressive — which[might include](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/16/upshot/michigan-progressives-el-sayed.html) much of the mainstream of the Democratic Party, not just factional candidates of the progressive left — progressives didn’t merely perform well but may have also found a way forward for a divided party.
